title: Blessing the house
hook: many churches bless homes at Epiphany or when people move in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the icon corner, a small place at home set apart for prayer. Your line was a corner of heaven. Did you set one up, even with one object? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

What's that written above the door? Over a front door, in white chalk, there's a short line of numbers and letters with little crosses between them. It went up one winter afternoon, while someone stood on a kitchen chair. A few streets away, a couple has just carried the last box into a new apartment, and their pastor stands in the empty living room, reading a short passage aloud. Across town, an Orthodox priest moves from room to room with a sprig of green dipped in water, sprinkling the walls, the beds, the stove. Three homes. One old habit, done three ways. Today: blessing the house.

Begin with the words. When Jesus sends his followers out to the towns in Luke's Gospel, he tells them what to do at the door. In the King James Bible: "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house." First. Before the teaching, before supper, before anything. And he adds that if a person of peace lives there, the peace will rest on them, and if not, it will come back to you. Nothing is wasted. Next, the chalk. Around Epiphany, the feast of the wise men, some Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran households mark the door in chalk with the year and three letters. Tradition says the letters stand for the names later given to the wise men, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, and also for Latin words asking Christ to bless the house. Matthew's Gospel says the wise men came to a house: "when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother." The chalk remembers a house where Christ was found. Then, the water. Orthodox churches bless water at Theophany, the feast of Christ's baptism, and afterward priests visit homes to sprinkle it through each room, with prayers for the people who live there. Other churches bless a home when a family moves in, walking it room by room. Last, a house in the Gospels that changed. Zacchaeus, a tax collector the crowd grumbles about, climbs a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus invites himself over. By the end, Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house." Not to the bricks. To the man, and the household. That's what these blessings are aiming at. Walls don't need peace. The people who argue in that kitchen and make up in it do. A blessing asks that this ordinary place, with its dishes and doorframes, be a place where God is welcome.
screen: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless each room. If you can, get up and walk slowly through your home. If you can't, walk it in your mind. Pause at the front door. Then each room in turn: the kitchen, a bedroom, the bathroom too. In each one, think of what happens there, and who. Meals. Sleep. Arguments. Making up. If you pray, you can say at each doorway the words Jesus gave his followers: Peace be to this house. If you don't, let each pause be a wish of peace for whoever lives in that room. End where you started, at the door. The bell holds the time.
Blessing the house. Asking God's peace on a home and the people in it, with words, chalk or water.
Your line: peace to this house. Today, when you come through your own front door, stop for one breath on the threshold before you go in. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Some Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran households chalk their doors at Epiphany; Orthodox priests visit homes with water blessed at Theophany; and other churches offer a house blessing when a family moves in.

what a scholar hears: Luke 10:5, "first say, Peace be to this house," and Zacchaeus in Luke 19: salvation comes to a house when it comes to the people in it.
